Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

div1.head: Interview with John O. Young, Jr. [6/8/2004]

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Today is June 8th, 2004. We are at the Warhawk Air Museum in Nampa, Idaho. Today we are privileged to be able to interview J.O. Young as part of the Veterans History Project in partnership with the Library of Congress. My name is Tim Peterson. I will be conducting the interview. Also present in the room is Jan Peterson who will be the director and camera person. J.O., can you please tell us your full name?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: John O. Young, Junior. And I've gone by J.O. all my life.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Okay. And what is your current address?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: [address redacted].

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: And what war were you involved in?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: World War II.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: World War II. Thank you very much. J.O., where were you born?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Nampa, Idaho, in the old Mercy Hospital on 16th Avenue South.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: So you grew up right here in Idaho?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Yes. Got away a few times but always drifted back.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: And you went to high school here in Nampa?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Graduated from the old Nampa High in 1940.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: And what did your parents do?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Dad was a superintendent for Morrison-Knudsen for about 30 years. So we lived all over the west wherever dad happened to be working. I went to 11 schools getting through 12 grades. So we moved frequently, not just to avoid the rent but because of the -- because of the work.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Understood. And did you end up going on to college here?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: No. No. At 19 I was a journeyman carpenter, and I had worked in the old Nampa Grocery in '39 and '40 after school. And then in the early part of 1941 I worked full time in the grocery store making $15 a week. And dad was superintendent at Gowen Field, building a couple of warehouses for Morrison-Knudsen. So when I got fired at the grocery store, I don't remember what the incident was, it was some silly thing, but I went over and went to work for dad. And I was making top wages, carpenter wages, $1.125 an hour, making $57.91 a week, and knew you could never spend that much money. No way. Pearl and I used to, that's my wife, we used to go to the movie which was 35 cents, and then we'd go to the Blue Bird and all shops down on Main Street, and milkshakes and hamburgers were 10 cents apiece. For a dollar and a dime we could have a great evening. And if we only had a dollar, we'd split the hamburger or the milkshake. Anyway, it was a different time of life.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: So you met your wife in high school?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Yes. Yeah. Her name was Pearl Sparks, and that was the gag at school. Pearl Sparks, oh, does she? Yeah, we -- we grew up together. We were both LDS, and I really didn't know her too much as a little girl, but when we started -- I lived one winter up in New Meadows with an old friend of the family on a fox farm and went to school at Meadows High. And then in my junior year I came down, and I met Pearl, and she had a girl friend that was a cute little thing, and I was madly in love with her girl friend, and then her girl friend moved to Burley. And the three of us during school, we'd walk all around talking and so forth. And after this other girl left, why, Pearl and I just kept on walking, and we're working on our 59th year now.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Oh, congratulations. That's wonderful. And you eventually joined the Navy?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: I was never -- I was never in the service. You can see that, I'm a Navy E-4 there, but I'll have to explain that.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: There were about 1,125 or 30 civilian workers on Wake Island working for Morrison-Knudsen, and when the war started there were about 350 Marines. I was at the canteen -- Well, let me back up. Two days before the war started, why, the carpenter superintendent come in and says, Any of you know how to drive a truck? And I said, Well, I've driven a pickup. He said, Fine, you go with Murdock and learn how to drive his truck. And what I did for two nights then was drive the truck unloading the ship that was bringing supplies to Wake Island. So 6:00 that morning we get the word that Pearl Harbor was bombed and, of course, we don't know anything about what's going on. And about noon, about 10, 15 minutes to 12 I was at the canteen, and we heard these planes coming in and, of course, we just thought they were our own planes. And we all ran out onto the parade ground to look over toward the airport, and the airport started going up in flames. They were bombing. And then as the planes got closer, why, there was kind of a tat-tat-tat-tat-tat, and they were machine gunning us. There was dust flying up all around us, and I made about a 100-yard dash to the lagoon and hid down behind some coral. And, of course, if a bomb had hit, it would have been like shooting fish in a well, but we escaped that. But these planes flew over. The China Clipper had left for Guam that morning. When it heard the news, it turned around and jettisoned its gas and landed again, and the Japs hit it a few times with machine guns but didn't put it out of commission. But they bombed the hotel, just destroyed the Pan American Hotel. And we just after the bombing, a group of us got in a bunch of big concrete pipe and sat there and talked and wondered what we were going to do. And in a couple hours, why, we got out and walked down to the landing where the -- where the China Clipper was, and they were trying to find the passengers, and they never did find all of them. A few of them wound up as prisoners. But a bunch of us are standing there, and the pilot says, There's room for a few more, any of you want to get in, anyone want to go on? Not a one of us did. Oh, no, Uncle Sam will be right here to get us, and that kind of remarks, and we'll be fine. And I didn't want to get on because my uncle, Forrest Reed, was on the island with me. He had been there since May, and I hadn't seen him since the bombing, so I didn't know what happened to him. But nobody got on the plane, nobody left, and we went back down towards camp. And the Marines were loading an ammunition truck, so we helped load the truck, rode over to Wilkes Island, and that's where we stayed. And we fought with the Marines for the 16 days that the Japanese attacked us. And on the third day, the 11th, the Japanese came in to take the island, and we had 5-inch guns on each island and a set of antiaircraft, three antiaircraft on each island. And we were -- I started out on the 5-inch gun, and then the second day a 500-pound bomb hit real close, knocked the sights off the gun and everything. So I went with my uncle and the other fellows over onto the 3-inch guns. But these Japs come in, and one of the Japanese ships came in, whether it was a cruiser or what it was, I don't know, but it got within about 4,500 yards of the island, and they opened up on them with the 5-inch guns. The commander of our gun was a fellow named Gordon, so we called him Flash Gordon, and he sighted, he bore sighted, he said, I think I'm on it, and fired and Peale Island fired about the same time. So whether both of us hit it, we don't know which hit it. Anyway, it sunk in four-and-a-half minutes. It must have hit the ammunition section of it or something. Anyway, we ran them off that day. We won Wake Island, we won the first war, the first battle of the war. And I don't remember, there was two or three ships sunk, and it was an interesting day. And then they bombed us for the next 15 days, 14 days, whatever it was until the 23rd. We were bombed 14 days out of the 16 days. But when they landed on the island on the 23rd, it was about, oh, probably 4:00 in the morning. It was pitch dark. We had our two search lights on out into the -- looking out into the surf, and the Japs immediately shot those out. We were half a dozen of us were passing ammunition to the -- to the 3-inch gun, and the fuse was set at 19 seconds, so we were shooting out way, way out into the surf. And I finally cut the fuse down to zero, and Gunner McKinstry who was in charge of the guns started screaming at us, Muzzle blast, we'll have a muzzle blast. Well, it didn't, but we never hit anything. But there were 72 Japanese landed on Wilkes Island, and we had as far as I know about 16 Marines, and eight of those were killed, but 70 of the Japanese were killed. And this CB McKinstry, Gunner McKinstry, was about 6 foot 4, weighed 260 pounds or so, and he went around with his .45 and was shooting these Japanese to make sure they were dead. And, of course, he got his share before they were down. But after we fired as long as we could, then we were commanded to drop back, and we went back and hid under a drug line until dawn. And then when we got out at dawn, why, we all went to get rifles. Japanese never took prisoners, and we just figured we were going to fight as long as we could last. And when I went over to get my rifle, why, here was a Japanese Marine and an American Marine impaled on their bayonets. And Gunner McKinstry told me about it later, he said he had just emptied his gun and was putting a clip back in his .45 and he saw this Jap up on this little mound starting to bayonet this soldier in the back, and Gunner McKinstry screamed, and the soldier turned around, and they both impaled each other. And the reason the gun misfired, because McKinstry didn't get the clip in, the clip seated. So that was a ghastly sight. But there were dead Jap Marines all over. And we just -- I got a rifle and a gun belt, and we were headed down towards the channel that separated Wilkes from Wake, and we just got a few hundred yards and here was a column of Japanese coming with Major Devereux in the lead with a white flag. So I threw away my gun, and I had on a shirt that had corporal stripes, and I threw it away because if they'd have known we were guerrilla fighters, why, they would have shot us right then. But anyway, they took us to the airport, and we spent all day at the airport. And they had three machine guns lined up in front of us, and we just supposed they were going to start shooting, and we discussed whether we should get up and run into them or just lay down or what to do. And as I remember, we weren't -- I suppose there was some fear there, but I mean you were there, there was nothing you could do, so you just had to try to figure out what the best thing was to do. And then several of these Japanese officers going around polishing their swords and figured, well, that might be part of the act too, but come to find out what they were doing, they were wiping the saltwater off of their swords. When they landed and came in through the surf, why, their sword scabbard got all wet. And so we spent the day, and then that night they shoved a thousand of us into a hangar that would hold maybe 500. And those in the back, some fellows passed out from lack of air, and there was no way of laying down. You just stood there. And then the next day they took us back to the barracks, and we were just Japanese labor until the 12th when they took us off. And the morning of the attack when we could see over the compound, the Stars and Stripes were -- were flying. I hope I can keep from getting emotional. And just not too long afterwards a white flag was flying, probably a bed sheet. And then later on in the day, why, the Rising Sun was flying. And a couple of days later we were marching in detail and marched past where the officers had their barracks, and here wadded up in a fish net was the American flag being used as a doorstop, and you just can't imagine what that does to you, desecrating the flag like that. But the thing that we found out was that when Old Glory doesn't fly, there's no freedom. That's the main thing. So we had different jobs that they had us do, unloading rice off the ships, and there were 100-kilo sacks which I think was about 125 pounds, I'm not sure. Anyway, two Japanese would pick up a sack of rice and put on your shoulders, and they did that to me, and I fell down. I couldn't -- I couldn't pack that much weight. I was -- I was 19 years old, 6 foot tall and weighed 119 pounds when I got on the island.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Oh, boy.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: So as you can realize, in school I wasn't in athletics. I was in the drama and newspaper. But anyway, it was an entirely different experience. And then 14 days on the ship to China, and the first couple of days it was steaming hot, and then it started getting cold. This was in January. And the farther north we got, the colder it got. And they threw a blanket down to each of us. Four of us decided, well, we can get close together and put all these four blankets over us and keep warm. When the Japs saw that, why, they immediately started screaming, and we had to break apart, wrap up what we could in this blanket. But it was a miserable trip. And the morning and night we got a little bowl of barley, and probably it wouldn't have been over a tablespoon of dry barley. It was just kind of a grew. And I think once or twice we got a daikon, daikons are long radishes that they do some kind of preserving in salt, and get one cup of water a day. And it was a miserable situation. Some of the fellows didn't have a bowel movement for the 14 days we were on the ship. So it was -- it was not nice. And we never got to leave the hold. They had these 5-gallon cans for latrines, and about half the guys were seasick and diarrhea and everything else, and they'd pull them up once a day and empty them. It was not a nice situation.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Did they give the duty to pulling up the latrines to the prisoners?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Yes. It was somebody who was in an upper -- We were on the bottom number one hold, so we never did get out. We stopped in Yokohama for two days, and we never -- we never got on deck. And on those -- that two days that we were in Yokohama, one of the Japanese got five of the Marines up on deck, and they were beheaded, and he was later hung.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: And he beheaded these guys?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Yes. There were four or five of them, they all beheaded these Marines.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Because the Japanese were killed on Wake. They were just -- So it was -- it was not a great ride. And then it took us I think four days to get to China, and it was in the evening just about dark, and it was about 6 kilometers to this Woosung which was the first prison camp we were in, and it was raining, and we were marched in there. And we had 36 men to a section. Pardon me. I was in barracks 3, section 6, and there was an aisle went between, and then there were two rows of men on each side. And I had about an 18-inch mattress, about 6 feet long, and that was our living quarters, and we had one blanket and a sawdust pillow. And we never in any of the camps, we never had any fire in the wintertime. So it was a miserable situation. And that first night they brought us in a bowl of rice, and I took one bite and bit into a big chunk of curry, and I couldn't eat any more. That just killed me, that hot curry. And that's the only time they ever served it was that first day. But we would get a bowl of rice in the morning and a bowl at night. And those that worked out -- I was a camp daiku or carpenter for about the first six months. I built coffins and repaired barracks and so forth. But the other prisoners were building Mount Fujiyama they called it, and they were digging out and piling this dirt high. They were going to go 21 kilometers. And I think they finally finished it, and we left before they did, but they finally finished it, but what it was was a rifle range they were building, and that was hard work digging and pushing these carts up the hill and so forth. It was not the best of times, and people did anything they could to keep from working or get into the hospital and get some rest of some kind. A group of the guys decided that they'd get circumsized, and if they got circumsized they could spend 15 days in the hospital. Well, shortly after being circumsized they repented, but very painfully, but it was -- it was funny. Dr. Kahn (phonetic) was the doctor. He was a Navy doctor. He was the one that did the circumcisions, and they named him the China clipper. Our Japanese doctor was a Dr. Shindel (phonetic), wonderful wonderful man. He did everything he could for us. The first appendicitis operation, why, he did with a straight razor and sewed him up with black thread, and he survived. And sometime in '42, I don't remember just when it was the date, but I had an appendicitis attack, and they took me in, and they didn't have any anesthetic of any kind, and they shot me four or five times and deadened the area and then cut open. It was a little painful, and when they started cutting the appendix out, it was kind of like cutting gristle. But as you can see, I recovered too. We had fairly good hospital facilities, not real good but -- They brought out some equipment that had been repatriated, some English doctors, different ones. I got the hives one day, and I went over to sick bay, and they gave me a shot of digitalis, and the hives went away immediately. And in a couple of hours here they were again, so I went back and they gave me another shot. The third time I went back, they said this is all you can have. You can't have any more of this. So they gave me the third shot of digitalis. And in the evening when the gates closed, why, I couldn't get back to the sick bay, so here came the hives again. And I went over to where they had a corpsman for sick bay inside the compound, and I told him, showed him what was happening. He said, Well, I'm not supposed to do this, but he reached up on the top of the shelf and got down his doctor bag and gave me two blue pills and a white one. And when he turned around to put the bag up, I just swallowed the three pills. And when he turned around he said, Now, when you get back to the barracks, you take the two blue pills, and if that doesn't put you to sleep, take the white one. Well, I got back to the barracks, I think. Anyway, when I woke up the next morning, I didn't have hives. It was silly. And the corpsman would put a fly in the top of a bottle of alcohol and tell the Japs it was contaminated and couldn't be used, and the Japs would say, Okay, throw it away. And, of course, they'd take the fly out and they'd drink it. It was their source of alcohol at the time.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: When you had the hives, you didn't have difficulty breathing?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Just a skin reaction?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Just a skin reaction. I don't know what it was. And then I -- they gave me shots for diphtheria, which I didn't have but for some reason they decided I should have shots, and that was in the fanny. And I don't think they used an 8-penny nail, but it was the old needles that you sharpened, you know. Oh, I can still feel that. You look back and it's funny. It was not funny then. There was very little humor. We got along. The Japanese could never figure out, for instance, I whistled all the time, and every once in a while, Oh, why you whistle? You're a prisoner, you're not supposed to whistle. And it was that kind of thing. In the evenings, why, the fireflies would be out, and you weren't supposed to smoke. Being a Mormon boy, of course I didn't smoke, but some of the fellows would grab a firefly and put it up to their mouth, and the Jap guard if he was around would run over and, No cigarette, no nothing. But they had their fun. You had to have a sense of humor or you wouldn't have survived. And while we were in Woosung, why, there was about five or six Red Cross boxes that we finally got, the Japanese ate most of them, but there was -- they were little five or six-pound boxes with a little can of clam, powdered milk, coffee, tobacco, yeah, two cigarettes, cocoa and butter and some sardines and different things. And somebody got a list of what was going to be in the first boxes, so as soon as I found out what was in it, why, I immediately traded my coffee for cocoa to somebody because I never did drink coffee. And that was a mistake because coffee and the cigarettes were the most important part of the package. You could trade a can of coffee for maybe two cans of food. And the cigarettes, that was -- that was like having a million dollars. You could trade those for anything. The sickest I ever got, and this was in Osaka, I traded three cigarettes for three fish heads, and they turned out to be rotten.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Oh, no.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Oh, I was sick. I thought I was going to die, but I didn't.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: You said the doctor was -- the Japanese doctor was fairly kind.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Oh, he was great.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Were there other Japanese that showed signs of humanity?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Yes. Most of the soldiers unless they had some rank were fit to be around. I mean, they were usually pretty good fellows. I think as the old saying goes, when they get a little authority, they begin to exercise unrighteous dominion, and that's what the officers did. I was -- I was the first one that got beat up when we got to Shanghai, to Woosung. And the morning after we got there, why, I was outside and came in and here the fellows were bringing their ticks back from across the road and they had been filling them with straw. So I grabbed mine, went over and filled it, came back, and laid it down. And about that time here come -- we nicknamed him Rocky, this guard, and the mistake I made was not noticing that he had come through and marked all the ticks that he thought needed a little more straw with a blue X with chalk and, of course, when mine didn't have a chalk mark on it, why, then he stood up and started beating me. And the only thing fortunate was they didn't hit like you would like an American would hit. They hit sideways, this way. They hit you on both sides of the head. It hurt like a son of a gun, but it wasn't -- it wasn't as bad as a blow that would have been struck. But it brought you right up tight. And it was everybody was going to kill all the Japs and so forth, but it was a daily occurrence from then on. Somebody was always getting pounded on for something. And then if one man had fouled up, they'd march us all out, line us up and stand at attention for two or three or four hours, whatever. It didn't make any difference whether it was summer or winter. So one man did something, everybody was guilty. So it -- it wasn't -- it wasn't the best of years. They served the food, the rice, in about a 5-gallon bucket, and the one that served the rice would put it in a bowl and scrape the top off. You couldn't pat it down or anything, you just had to put it in and scrape it off. And if there was any left, why, they'd take a griswold cup and fill it and then cut it in two and give a little to each fellow. And I was on the -- I was in charge of the soup bucket. I eventually got the name King of the Ladle. And the soup was usually seaweed or maybe some a little fish or something, very very little meat of any kind. But you had to stir it up each time, and you had to start with a different man each time, so that everybody would eventually get the same amount of solids if you could -- if you could do it. But we were living on as we figured from 600 to 900 calories. And a lot of the fellows, they lost more than they weighed. In other words, my friend George Denton from Boise weighed 210 pounds when he came in, and when he left, when he got out he was 98 pounds. And for me for some reason in those three years, I had gained a little weight. I weighed 128 pounds when I got out. I don't know whether it was just from growing or what. But then on the way home it was -- it was unreal. No one ever said a word about what we should eat or what we shouldn't eat, and it's a wonder some of us didn't die because when we landed on Guam, there were a thousand of us. We landed there at lunchtime and ate 4,000 men's rations, and then we repeated that at suppertime and ate 4,000 men's rations. And we had chicken ala king which was rich anyway, and we ate all that we could hold. And then when we were through, in front of me was about a half a loaf of bread and a can of milk and sugar, and I ate all of that. And in about 30 minutes I was going both ends. I was sick the four days I was on Guam. I don't know whether it was green or a desert or what Guam was, but it's a wonder some of us didn't die. I gained 60 pounds on the way home in that 30 days.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Good golly.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: I was just -- and my wife was real scared because she brought my suit but didn't bring a belt, but I didn't need a belt. I don't know how I ever got in the suit. We landed in San Francisco, I think it was either the 2nd or 3rd of October, and Forrest Packard and I were standing on the rail, and there were all these people out on the dock waiting, and Forrest Packard was from Meridian. They had 17 children, and I don't know whether you saw that on the news the other night or not, but they had a little story on his family. But he was standing there and pretty quick, Oh, there's my queen, and he rushed out and got down. And there was some little blonde in a red dress waving at somebody, and I finally realized it was my girl Pearl, and she and mother had come to meet me. And so I went down and fortunately I went and hugged and kissed Pearl first before I did mother. Pearl says now if he's going to kiss her first, he probably don't think that much of me, so it was a good thing that I made the right choice. But it was -- we were going to be married in October of 1941, and I was working for J.O. Jordan here in Boise on the old Salt Lake Hardware. And it rained one afternoon, and another old carpenter and I got in under the shed and we got to talking about Wake Island. A lot of the fellows had gone over. And Morrison-Knudsen was right across the street. So we walked across, and we were hired on the spot. He didn't pass the physical, so he didn't go, but I did. Left on the 17th or 16th, whatever it was, 16th I guess, yeah, of September. And six of us left Boise at that time and went to Alameda, and then was put on the SS Mariposa, a luxury liner, and went on to Honolulu. Going down to Los Angeles that first night, the ground swelled, I got just a little nauseated, but that was the only time. I never did get seasick from then on. When we got within two days of Wake, we got into the tail end of a typhoon, and you could sit on the deck and those waves were 30 feet above you, you know, and I never got seasick again. Anyway, we had lots of experiences.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: While you were in the camp, news about the war, did you get any?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Very, very little. The letters were all sensored, but we got one -- one fellow got a letter that said Your Uncle Sammy had a great time on Midway -- no -- had a party on Midway. Had a great time. So we realized that something good had happened. He didn't have an Uncle Sammy, so it had to be Uncle Sam. So we knew something good had happened on Midway. And then one fellow got a letter that said, Your Aunt Allis-Chalmers is having a baby every seven minutes. So we knew that -- as a matter of fact during that time stuff was going good. But we got little information. One fellow was able to put a little radio together at one time, and we got a little news for a while, but it was not much. And then they found it, and we all stood at attention for five or six hours, and they tore up the radio, of course. It's no wonder they didn't shoot him, but they didn't.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Did the Japanese allow you to write back?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: We could write once in a while. You mean as far as letters are concerned?

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. In fact, in here there's a letter or two or three of mine that I did get home. And I only got two or three letters from home. In fact, the first letter I got was Thanksgiving Day of 1942, I got a letter from mother and from Pearl. Those were -- those were good letters.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Now, how did you get the news that the war was over?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: We lined up to go to work. We were up in (inaudible). I was working in a steel mill at that time, and we were lined up ready to go to work and in come the day crew and the Jap guard says, Today no shoku gyou. No work. And the lights -- the power's off at the plant. And then one of the fellows said one of the Jap guards had told him the war was over, he was going to get a sock full of rice and head for the hills. So it was two or three days before we knew for sure, but the guards quit beating on us and we didn't have to salute them, and pretty quick they were all gone. And a couple of -- several days later a couple of Navy fighter planes flew over and wiggled their wings and let us know that they knew we were there. And then in a few hours they came back and dropped duffel bags and jeans with the legs and the top tied together with cigarettes and candy and magazines and different things like that. And my uncle and I went through the whole four years and never got a scratch. And when these planes come over and dropped these bags, he was sitting on a fence and had to jump off to keep from getting hit and broke his ankle.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: So he was all -- in about six days he got to go home. And then it was the 6th of September before we got on the train to -- we went down to Yokohama, and I have never seen anything like it was going through Tokyo. The only thing that was intact was the railroad line. On each side as far as you could see there might be an old chimney or a safe or something sticking up, but there must have been millions of people killed. They just destroyed the whole city. And the greatest thing that happened in World War II was dropping those two atomic bombs. If they hadn't, there would have been millions and millions killed on both sides because the Japanese at the end of the war had about 5,000 planes stored, were making I think it was 162 they said a month, and they had armed the population as near as they could, and each one of those -- each one of those planes that they had would have been kamikaze type planes. And if it hadn't have been for the atomic bombs, no telling how many million would been killed. It would have been a complete disaster. And you hear these idiots talk about how terrible the atomic bombs were. They weren't there. And of course, we didn't know anything about them from our camp. We didn't know anything about the atomic bombs until we got back stateside or back on the ship where we could talk to someone who did. But there was lots of interesting experiences. And it separates the men from the boys. There were some that were conniving and doing everything they could to stay alive, and they didn't care what they did to anyone else to do so. And one of the fellows, and I can't remember his first name but his last name was Keach, and he lived in Homedale, but he starved to death because he traded all his rice for cigarettes, and he just simply starved to death. His brother's name was Itchy (phonetic) Keach, and I had to conduct his funeral when he came home, and committed suicide not too long after we got home.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Now, were there other prisoners of war from other countries in your camp?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: In Woosung, the first camp, they brought in about 20 British that they had gotten off a ship or something. So on most of the camps we had a few people from other countries, either English or Australian or Indonesian. And of course, the Indonesians were all black but they all called themselves Dutch because Indonesia was a Dutch province at that time.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Now, you brought in some photos, and the first photo we have here is Wake Island.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Okay. I'm going to hold that up. It's not a very big island, is it?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: It's about 7 1/2 miles from tip to tip, and half a mile wide in the widest point, and 22 feet in the highest point. Wilkes and Peale Island were discovered by explorers of that name. And I think Wake was a Navy captain or something that sailed in there in the 1800s.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: I'll be darn. And then below here is the Japanese ship.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: That's the Nitta Maru, that's the one we went to Japan on -- went to China on rather.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: You were in the --

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: In the number one hold of that.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: The bottom of the ship.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: So you learned about what runs downhill.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: And how many days did it take you to get to --

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: 14 days.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: 14 days I think you said.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: 14 days on that ship.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: And then on the --

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: That just gives you a little clearer picture of what the island looked like.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Wake Island. Okay. And then we have --

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: This was out of the Statesman in April of '42 or 3, whatever it was.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: This says 1942.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: I don't know the other two fellows. I don't remember them.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: It says, These Idaho -- correction -- These Idaho youths believed Jap prisoners. So you never met these guys after you got back?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: I might have known them on the island, but I don't remember them.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: When I -- When I decided to go to Wake, why, I went home, I was living in Boise with my folks, went to Nampa, went out to the farm, picked up Pearl, and she snuggled up to me, and we headed into town to go to the show, and I told her what I was going to do, that I decided that I would go for nine months and come home with $2,000. And that was a lot of money in those days, when a dollar was a dollar. And as soon as I said that, why, she scooted over to the other side of the car on the driver's side and sat there and grumbled the rest of the evening. Finally she decided it was all right, that nine months wouldn't be too bad. If she would have known it would have been four years, I'm not sure what she would have thought. But she waited. Nine children and 40 grandchildren later, why, not too bad.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: This is one of your letters.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Yes. See, that was barracks 3, section 6, Shanghai prisoner of war. And you had to write -- you couldn't say what's going on. It is a pleasure to be able to write you folks again. Next to getting home is the best thing that could happen would be a letter from you folks. Mom, you and Carol have nothing on me. The 12th of last month I went under -- oh, that's when I had my operation. 12th of last month I went under for an appendectomy which was a complete success. Patient recovered. We are very fortunate to have the fine medical staff we have. I think of you folks at home a lot and hope and pray you are all in the best health as I am. That was baloney. I can't imagine reading Dale, that's my brother, grown men probably cutting cards or flipping the coin to see who gets the car for the night. Doubt if I can ever drive anymore. By the way, mom, you had better brush up on your crib game, so as you'll be a little competition when I get home. I played a little bit of crib, but I wasn't a card player. The next card I'll write to Pearl. Dad, you better take a day off and go trout fishing for me. Kind of think I'll do my own fishing next year. Well, folks, until that certain day, keep a light in the window for your Prodigal Son.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Very good.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: I don't know why I can't handle those.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: That's okay. It's okay.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: That was my friend, Lloyd Nelson there, and that's what we looked like.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: I'll bring that up here.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: In the camps I was in, there were never any pictures taken.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Now, he has a number pinned on him.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Yes. That was his prison camp number. I was 116 in China and 541 in Japan, that is in Osaka.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Okay. And then you brought in a flag, a photograph of a flag.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Don't show that one. We'll show the other one.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Okay. Before we get to the second flag, this is kind of interesting, tell us about this. This looks like --

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Well, what it is are our Japanese records that they had in the various prison camps, and they're on both sides of the page. Not being able to read Japanese, of course, I can't tell you what it says. One is Forrest Reed.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: So you have yourself here and you have your uncle.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Uncle Forrest Reed on the back side. I remember that now.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: So they had your date of birth. Employee of contractor, Pacific Naval Air Base, Wake Island.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: For your uncle, and they say the same thing on yours. And I'm amazed that they kept records like this. And you say this is back in Washington, D.C.?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Yes, that's in the archives.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: In the archives. So people that want to research that can go find this information.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Wow, that's really something.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: And that's just another letter.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: That you wrote home.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Okay. And another letter that you wrote home.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: That letter was written from Kiangwang. We were in Woosung for nine months, and then ten months in Kiangwang which is just a few miles, 6 kilometers or something from Woosung.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: The last paragraph here on this letter is: I can tell you how much I love you and how much I think of you. Best, I just have to keep hoping and praying that this war will terminate soon. So long until then. Question mark. Your son and sweetheart. J.O. Nice ending.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: We had a hard time being optimistic all the time, and we didn't want to be pessimistic, and couldn't be optimistic all the time, so I coined the word hopetimistic. We hoped that good things were going to happen.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Hopetimistic.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Hopetimistic.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: I like that word. And here this --

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: This was a picnic we had at Twin Falls.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: And when you say we had a picnic --

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: The Wake Island group.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: The Wake Island group. I'm going to take this out and hold this up. In 1957.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Uh-huh. Got anything on it or do you have to be closer?

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Okay. Let me put that back. Here's the second flag.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Now, that's the flag that was made by Sclutz and T. Bailey Lee, and the red material was stolen from the Japanese and the white was from bed sheets that they were able to scrounge in the barracks and the blue was from some English gave him the blue for the background for the flag, and they worked 26 hours putting that together, and then they flew it over their camp. And it's in the Boise Museum now.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: And they started flying in their camp. So it's really true, as you said earlier, if Old Glory doesn't fly, then there's no freedom.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Oh, there's no freedom. No.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: So Old Glory was flying again --

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: -- and you had freedom. Okay. And here we have a drawing?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Yes, that's a drawing by this Wattles and this is the cook shack. That's where they cooked the rice.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Okay. Get a shot of that.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: And then the other picture is the water tower, and he drew too nice a picture of that. It was an old leaky water tower that was about to fall over, but he drawed it there so it looks real good.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Okay. And then here we have --

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: That was the Christmas menu for 1941.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Which, of course, we never had.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: You never made it.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Never made it.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: So we've got the nice front of the menu here, and you actually have what you were going to have.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Yes. There was the menu there.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Here's the actual --

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: It was a very fine meal that they were having. In fact, we had excellent food on Wake Island, all you could eat and everything.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: It says here you were going to have pearl onions, Hawaiian fruit cup, cream of chicken, grilled filet of sole, of course turkey, cranberry sauce, quite a few deserts including various cheeses. It sounds like it was going to be a pretty nice meal.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: It was going to be a fine meal. That's just a picture of me by my car showing the license plate which I don't think will show up on the camera.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: I think that was back here.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Somehow I got the car out of sequence. This is something else?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Oh, well, that's just one of our gatherings.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Okay. When you got back to the States, tell us about that day.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Well, it was a great day, one we had been hoping for for four years almost. And the interesting part of it was I knew I was coming home to marry my girl. I knew that everything had been all right. There hadn't been any deaths that I knew of. And I just came home, went to work, we got married a month after I got home, started having our nine children, and I never even thought about the war. Never even thought about hating the Japanese or anything like that. And it's interesting because a lot of the fellows still to this day just can't stand the Japanese, they hate them. In fact, a few years ago in the Letters to the Editor in the Statesman, one of my friends wrote and he just couldn't say enough bad things about the Japanese, and I never even thought about them afterwards. I just came home and started living. And, of course, my church had a lot to do with it, being LDS, why, you're busy all the time if you want to be. And I was a bishop and on the High Council and so forth and was in leadership in the church for many years, and you just didn't have time to think about these silly things. And you hear about these people that come home and have to go to the psychiatrist and everything and all of the problems they had, and there were some that had problems. We had a few fellows from Wake that couldn't handle it when they got back. But I guess it just depends on what attitude you have and what you have to do.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: And tell us about your career after you got back.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Well, I was -- I was a journeyman carpenter, and I had $3,000 when I got home, and dad and I went into the construction business. We had J.O. Young and Sons for 15 years. And we went broke about the 15th year, we had a bad job up on the North Fork at Clearwater, and the company folded. And then I went into sales. I sold insurance for a while and worked at Blacker's for a while and different things. And then at retirement time, why, I did build a house down in Kingman, Arizona. We moved down to Bullhead City, and I finished the store over at Laughlin, a grocery store, and then the wife and I went on a mission and went to a Singapore mission for our church, and we were in Indonesia and Malasia for 18 months. And then when we came home, we were home about a year, and we were living in Kingman then. Our daughter and son-in-law that we were living with had moved to Kingman. And then we were there about a year, and then we went on another mission and went to the Puerto Rican mission and spent 18 months on St. Thomas, U.S. Virgin Islands. Both of them very fine experiences. But never did anything real exciting, just lived and let live.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Tell us about your nine kids, what are they doing today?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Well, we have seven living. The first -- my first son was going to be Michael Alan, and that was Janine. And then my second son was going to be Michael Alan, and that was Jolynn. And then Jana and Julie came along and finally John. We never did get a Michael Alan. We named all nine with the letter J. And John, like I say, died in September. And little Jana, she died of polio in 1952. So we have five children living, two here in town. Lamont and Jorjette Bostrom, she's our daughter. And they -- well, in July it will be 19 years ago they walked into the house, and they had this baby in their arms, and I said, Good heavens, what are you doing with a baby? Where did you get it? Oh, it's ours. Well, where did you get it? Some people gave it to us. And he was a Tongan baby, and the grandparents had raised two of the daughter's children but they didn't think she could raise a third one, so they adopted that little guy. And then in 19 -- about 1990, somewhere along in there, why, as we were leaving Kingman for our mission, why, they adopted a little black boy. And they have adopted four since. They have five black children and a little Tongan boy in their family. And then the other daughter, Jody, she and her husband live here in town, and he has a lawn business, and they have half a dozen children. And then Janine, the one who's the widow, she lives in Emmett. And we have a son who's a Swan truck driver that lives in Payette. And then our daughter Jolynn lives in Mountain Home. Her husband is a schoolteacher, been over there for 20 years or so at school. So we have five families in about a 100-mile radius which makes it real nice. We always have lots of help and lots of company. Sunday we had three families and three couples out of those families and all the grandkids, so the house was bouncing. We've got a small home. But we have a good family, good time. Enjoy them.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Well, J.O., I want to pan in the map before we leave just so that people can see where your journey took you during World War II. Of course, here we have the States.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Right here. And we have the Hawaiian Islands right here which everybody is familiar. And then just a tiny --

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: About 2,400 miles west is Wake Island.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Wake Island, and this is where you were captured here.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Right, that's where we were captured, and then we were taken right near Shanghai.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Which is right here.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: That's where the Kiangwang and Woosung camps were. And then we crossed over to Japan to Osaka.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Which is near Tokyo.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: And then in May of '45 we were bombed out of Osaka and went up north about 120 miles from Tokyo to a place called Naoetsu. And I have never found anyone that knew where Naoetsu was except when we were in Da Nang, Malasia, on our mission, we were on the beach, and there was a Japanese couple that were vacationing there, and I asked him about Naoetsu, and he knew where it was. That's the only person I ever knew -- ever met that knew where it was.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: J.O., is there anything that we've not covered during this interview that you would like to talk about?

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Probably but I don't know what it would be. We've talked about a lot of things. It's great to be an American, and these people that don't appreciate it, too bad they can't live somewhere else.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Well, I want to thank you for coming in today and sharing your recollections with us.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: Well, fine. Glad to be able to do so.

sp.speaker: Tim Peterson
sp.p: Thank you.

sp.speaker: John O. Young, Jr.
sp.p: More than welcome. [Interview concluded]
